summary:
ASTRA is an astronaut health self-assessment prototype that turns scattered daily readings into clear, traceable records. We built a React frontend and FastAPI backend to record blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, temperature, sleep and mood. Interactive charts, baseline comparisons, measurement guides and a selectable 3D body help users explore their records. Regions without measurements remain clearly marked as insufficient data.

ASTRA addresses the challenge of organizing health information when crews operate far from Earth with limited communication. Its backend rule engine owns classifications and alerts; optional AI explains supplied findings without changing them. During link loss, readings remain “pending—not evaluated” until synchronized. A simulated SOS workflow demonstrates local queuing, server receipt and delayed Earth acknowledgments.

The project matters because clear records, visible uncertainty and reliable handover can support better-informed conversations with medical personnel. ASTRA uses synthetic data throughout and is not medically validated, NASA-endorsed or a real emergency communication service.
details:
ASTRA—Astronaut Self-assessment, Tracking & Risk Analysis—is a decision-support prototype that helps users record health measurements, explore changes over time, and understand them in the context of spaceflight research. Developed for NASA Space Apps, it uses clearly labeled SIMULATED data. It is not medically validated or NASA-endorsed.

Users can record six indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, and mood. Each record can include its time, units, measurement method, and data quality. Progress charts compare readings with supplied personal baselines, preserve missing dates as gaps, and keep fasting and non-fasting glucose records separate. Habit logs and editable reminders support consistent recordkeeping without prescribing medical targets.

An interactive, procedural 3D body connects eight body regions to their available records, explanations, and evidence. Users can rotate the model or select regions through an accessible keyboard list and 2D fallback. Regions without measurements remain gray rather than suggesting that they have been assessed. Radiation records appear in a separate module, without personal risk estimates or invented dose limits.

ASTRA’s architecture separates decisions from explanations. In connected mode, a deterministic Python backend owns classifications, review flags, and escalation. Optional AI can explain approved findings but cannot change them; deterministic fallback text remains available when AI fails. The published demonstration uses scripted synthetic results and explanations, with clinical criteria inactive.

We built ASTRA using React, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei, supported by Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and Docker. Testing uses pytest, Vitest, React Testing Library, and Chromium browser checks. No specialized hardware is required for the demonstration; measurements are entered manually.

The project’s creative contribution is bringing visual body exploration, longitudinal records, plain-language explanations, and traceable spaceflight evidence into one interface. Its intended impact is to make records easier to understand and discuss with qualified medical personnel, including during simulated communication interruptions.

Our design decisions prioritize accessibility, uncertainty, privacy, and scientific honesty. We distinguish source-supported statements from project inferences, avoid diagnoses and treatment plans, and make missing data and prototype limitations visible. ASTRA demonstrates an approach to clearer recordkeeping and decision transparency; it does not claim proven medical outcomes or operational mission readiness.
